transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jon Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (Head of ML - Atlas), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng - Atlas), Priya Singh (CTO - Atlas)

Summary:
Redwood team walked Atlas Financial through Redwood Optimize focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations. Demonstrated cost model trade-offs for hosted vs dedicated, impact of batching & KV cache on token cost and latency, and outlined a POC plan for a dedicated benchmark. Security and networking questions (VPC, KMS) discussed; next steps include sending cost workbook and scheduling POC.

Topics covered:
- Workload characterization and QPS patterns
- Batching strategies (dynamic batching, max batch size, latency SLO implications)
- Prefix vs KV cache (hot prefix caching vs token-level KV caching)
- Cost model: tokens saved, GPU utilization, effective $/1M tokens
- Deployment choices: hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC)
- Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS/HSM, audit logs, SSO

Action items (captured above)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): "All right everyone, thanks for joining — we'll kick off. Quick intros? I'm Maya, AE on the Optimize team. Jon is our systems SE who runs the benchmarks.

[00:22] Sofia (Atlas): "Hi, I'm Sofia, Head of ML at Atlas, we own the recommendation stack. We've got a few questions about latency and cost, especially when we hit month-end peaks.

[00:35] Liam (Atlas): "Liam here, platform engineering. We'll own the POC networking and infra, mostly VPC peering and firewall rules.

[00:40] Priya (Atlas): "Priya here, quick note: security/compliance is a gating item for us. SOC2 plus KMS for keys.

[00:46] Jon (Redwood SE): "Great, thanks. Today we're going to show Optimize's recommendations — batching, prefix and KV cache behaviour, and a cost model so you can see dollars/Tokens saved. I'll do a short demo of the Console and then we can walk through numbers.

[01:10] Maya: "Before we jump in, can you share a bit about your traffic shape? Are you steady QPS or spiky?

[01:20] Sofia: "Mostly spiky. Baseline is ~80 QPS but we hit 1.2k for short bursts during report generation and end-of-day runs. Latency SLO is 150ms p95 for interactive flows, background batch flows can be 500ms.

[01:38] Jon: "That's helpful. So two workloads: interactive low-latency and background tolerant. We'll show how Optimize recommends different batching strategies for each and how KV cache can save tokens for repeat prefixes.

[01:55] [Demo start - Console screen share noise]

[02:10] Jon: "Here on the Console under Optimize -> Batching we profile a sample of your traffic (we used a synthetic trace based on the numbers you gave). The profiler shows sequence length distribution, prefix reuse, and tail latency contribution. You can see the histogram — a lot of short calls and then a long tail.

[02:38] Maya: "Key thing is batching knobs: target latency SLO, max batch size, and timeout window. If you increase the timeout to collect more requests you'll improve GPU utilization but increase p95 latency.

[02:56] Liam: "Do you have guidance on what timeout window to pick for 150ms SLO?

[03:05] Jon: "In practice for 150ms p95 we recommend a small timeout, 5-10ms with max batch sizes tuned to your QPS. For your baseline 80 QPS that maps to pretty small average batch sizes — maybe 4-8 tokens per batch. But during 1.2k spikes the runtime can form large batches which are more efficient — that's where dedicated capacity helps.

[03:38] Sofia: "How does prefix caching interact with batching? If I cache a common prefix like "customer_profile:" will that avoid generation?

[03:48] Jon: "Good question. Prefix cache stores the output for repeated prefix sequences so the runtime can short-circuit generation and return cached tokens. That reduces compute and latency massively for hot prefixes. KV cache is slightly different — it's the model KV state per session, used for longer context reuse; comes in handy for multi-turn chat or repeated context.

[04:10] Maya: "We sometimes call them prefex in our transcripts, you'll see mis- — but the distinction is: prefix cache is output-level cache, KV cache is internal key-value states to speed subsequent tokens.

[04:26] Jon: "In the console here, Optimize recommends prefix caching for the top 2% of prefixes that account for ~30% of tokens in your profile. Enabling that can lower token cost by ~18-25% in our sim.

[04:46] Priya: "What's the risk of stale data? If the underlying content changes, how do you invalidate the prefix cache?

[04:54] Jon: "You can set TTLs and also version keys. We recommend short TTLs for user-specific content and longer for static templates. Invalidation hooks can be called from your app via the API to evict keys. We'll share docs.

[05:10] Maya: "Now cost model. We built a simple workbook that converts tokens generated, tokens avoided (via cache), GPU seconds, and translates to effective dollars per 1M tokens. I'll walk through one scenario for hosted vs dedicated.

[05:28] Jon: "For hosted: we assume per-token pricing and some variance. For dedicated: you pay for reserved GPU time but you get better utilization because batching and caching raises throughput. In the example here, with your traffic mix and enabling prefix cache + 2x batching, dedicated reduces effective $/1M tokens by ~40% compared to hosted at peak.

[05:58] Sofia: "40% is compelling. Is that before or after data egress and other infra costs?

[06:03] Jon: "This model focuses on compute cost; we flag additional infra line items separately. We'll include connectors and egress in the workbook as line items you can toggle.

[06:15] Liam: "How sensitive is that 40% to sequence length? If we have longer sequences will gains be larger?

[06:22] Jon: "Generally yes — longer sequences mean more opportunity for caching and more benefit from batching on dedicated GPUs; also KV cache helps because you avoid re-computing earlier tokens in the KV state. But extremely long sequences can also hit memory limits; our Optimize tool will surface quantization recommendations if you need a smaller model footprint.

[06:46] [08:00-35 simulated time jump in transcript for demo steps]

[08:05] Jon: "Here's the simulated POC run results: baseline hosted no-cache p95 latency 170ms, hosted with prefix cache 130ms, dedicated with batching+KV cache 95ms p95. Token cost reductions aligned with what we said.

[08:28] Priya: "Those p95 numbers look good. For Dedicated, what's the SLO you include in the contract?

[08:35] Maya: "We offer SLA-backed latency and uptime targets for Dedicated; specific numbers depend on the capacity tier. We'll include the SLA table in the follow-up deck.

[08:46] Sofia: "What about multi-tenant isolation and data retention? We can't have customer data leave our VPC except for usage metrics.

[08:55] Jon: "For Private deployment we support a customer-managed control plane and on-prem package. For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and encryption at rest + KMS. We also support audit logs shipping to your SIEM.

[09:12] Liam: "Is HSM supported for key wrapping?

[09:15] Jon: "Yes, we integrate with customer KMS and HSM vendors; we'll attach the integration guide.

[09:25] Maya: "Back to Optimize: there's also dynamic batching where the runtime adapts batch windows by traffic phase. That way you get low latency during low QPS and high throughput during spikes without manual retuning.

[09:40] Sofia: "Can we set different policies per route? For example, interactive routes are strict, background routes are throughput-first.

[09:48] Jon: "Yes, per-route policies are supported in the Console — you can pin timeouts, max batch sizes, and caching rules per route. We showed a sample config in the demo.

[10:02] Maya: "One practical note: when you enable KV cache for sessions, you'll need to size for memory since KV states are per-session. Optimize will recommend eviction and TTL policies.

[10:18] Liam: "Does KV cache persist across restarts? If a worker dies do we lose the session?

[10:24] Jon: "KV is sharded in-memory for latency; we recommend using prefix cache or external session store for very long lived sessions. For Dedicated we do provide persistent KV options as part of the deployment.

[10:40] [11:30 - cost workbook walkthrough continued]

[11:35] Jon: "Here's a sensitivity chart: x-axis is QPS spike magnitude, y-axis is $/1M tokens. The gap between hosted and dedicated widens with bigger spikes because dedicated amortizes GPU fixed costs better.

[11:55] Sofia: "If we don't want dedicated yet can we still test caching benefits on hosted?

[12:02] Maya: "Absolutely — Optimize can run experiments on hosted. We'll give you a benchmark runbook to test prefix cache and measure token reuse and latency improvement.

[12:12] Priya: "What telemetry do you provide so we can validate improvements?

[12:18] Jon: "Console provides per-route token breakdown, cache hit rates, latency percentiles and cost attribution per route/model. There's also a tracing hook if you want full request traces.

[12:30] Liam: "Regarding networking, for the POC we'll need peering + firewall outbound rules. We'll send a diagram of our egress policy.

[12:40] Maya: "Great — we'll pair Jon with Liam for the runbook.

[12:46] [13:00 - Q&A flare, some cross talk, slight transcription errors]

[13:05] Sofia: "Are there any gotchas with tokenization differences between models? Sometimes our prompts tokenized differently and that skewed the cache hit estimate.

[13:15] Jon: "Yep, tokenization can affect cache granularity. Optimize runs tokenization-aware analysis and will surface where tokenization reduces hit rates. We sometimes recommend normalizing prompts or using a canonical prefix.

[13:30] Sofia: "Can you show the TTL controls in the Console?

[13:36] Jon: "Sure — here under Caching -> Prefix rules you can set TTLs per prefix and pattern-based eviction. Note you can also use API calls to evict specific keys on content change.

[13:50] Maya: "We'll include a short how-to in the follow-up.

[14:00] [18:00 - mid-demo pause, bench numbers, casual banter]

[18:05] Jon: "One scenario I want to call out: when you have high re-use of session context KV cache is huge, but it can increase memory footprint. Optimize recommends quantization profiles to keep the model in memory if needed.

[18:28] Liam: "Quantization — you support int8 and fp16?

[18:33] Jon: "Yes, we support mixed precision and several quantization profiles; Optimize suggests models and profiles based on latency/quality tradeoffs. We'll show sample evals in the workbook.

[18:50] Priya: "How do you validate quality regressions when quantizing?

[18:55] Jon: "We recommend a small eval set (we can help create it) and Redwood has quality monitoring to flag numeric regressions on prompt families. You can gate rollouts based on those metrics.

[19:10] Sofia: "If we do a POC on Dedicated, what metrics should we capture?

[19:16] Jon: "Token cost, p50/p95 latency, cache hit rates, GPU utilization, and end-to-end user-perceived latency are our core metrics. We'll provide the runbook template.

[19:32] Maya: "Ok wrapping toward next steps — we heard three asks: share cost workbook, set up POC runbook and schedule peering call.

[19:42] Priya: "Yes, and attach SOC2 + KMS integration docs.

[19:48] Maya: "We'll do that. Anything else?

[19:52] Sofia: "Can Redwood run a quick sim from our repo of prompts? We can share a sample dataset and have you run Optimize profile against it.

[20:00] Jon: "Yes, please send a representative sample (anonymized). We'll run profiling and return recommendations.

[20:08] Liam: "I'll gather traffic shapes and send tonight.

[20:12] Maya: "Great. Last thing — budget/contract timing?

[20:18] Priya: "We have budget cycles end of Q1, so ideally POC in March, a decision early Q2.

[20:26] Maya: "That aligns — we'll target the POC in March.

[20:30] [Wrap-up and informal sign-offs across the group]

[20:40] Maya: "Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the workbook and runbook, and Jon will coordinate POC details with Liam.

[20:48] Jon: "Thanks, talk soon.

[20:52] Sofia: "Thanks all.

[20:55] Priya: "Bye.

[21:00] End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional labels compressed, minor mis-hearings (prefex/prefix), some technical terms spelled out for clarity.
